newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor said calm on eve of Dili anniversary.
newsitem.headline: East Timor said calm on eve of Dili anniversary.

text.p: East Timor was calm but security was tight on Monday on the eve of the fifth anniversary of the deaths of at least 50 demonstrators shot by troops in the capital Dili, residents said.
"Things are still calm and we haven't had any problems, but the security is tight," one resident told Reuters by telephone from Dili.
In 1991, Indonesian troops fired on demonstrators making their way to the Santa Cruz cemetery from a church funeral for an anti-Indonesian youth activist who had been shot two weeks earlier.

A government investigation said later 50 people were killed in the incident, which prompted an international outcry. Witnesses and human rights groups estimate around 180 people were killed and many wounded.

Indonesia, with implicit Western backing, invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in December 1975 and incorporated it as its 27th province the following July in a move the United Nations has refused to recognise.

In past years, the anniversary has provided a focal point for opposition to Jakarta's rule. Last year it came amid a series of break-ins at foreign embassies in Jakarta by East Timorese seeking political asylum.

University students took to the streets in Dili last Thursday after a local man was stabbed by a trader from Sulawesi island, but university officials quickly calmed the situation and the students dispersed without further trouble, diplomatic sources and residents said.
"I don't think it was too important an incident, but it was a clear signal that everyone should keep quiet," a diplomatic source in close contact with East Timor said.
"There is an uneasy calm. While people are afraid of trouble that could be created by demonstrations, it doesn't mean people wouldn't like to commemorate the (1991) incident," he added.
Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo, regarded as one of the most influential people in East Timor who was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last month, has consistently appealed for calm.
Diplomatic sources said Belo told worshippers at a Mass on October 26 that demonstrations, violence and burnings must come to an end.
Belo himself flew to Jakarta on Monday and was expected to remain there until Thursday attending an annual meeting of Indonesian bishops in the capital, church officials said.
Belo has come under fire from officials in Jakarta for statements he is reported to have made in an interview with the the German news magazine Der Spiegel.
The official Antara news agency quoted him as having said in the interview that Indonesian troops had trampled on East Timor's independence "and treated us like dogs".
The bishop said in a statement that he would remain silent on the issue until he had seen the full text of the interview.

A conference on East Timor critical of Indonesia ended in chaos in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday after groups of youths allied to Malaysia's ruling coalition disrupted the gathering and police detained a number of activists.
The Malaysian government had condemned the conference as damaging to its relations with Indonesia.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters on Monday he appreciated the policy of the Malaysian government that regarded East Timor as an internal matter for Indonesia.
Alatas left with President Suharto on Monday for a week-long visit to Jordan and Italy.
